solution:
In every case the body is either at rest or moving with constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero and by Newton's first law the net force on it must be zero.
(a) The drop falls with constant speed, so its weight is exactly balanced by the viscous drag and buoyancy of the air. Net force \(= 0\).
(b) The cork floats at rest, so its weight is balanced by the upward buoyant force of the water. Net force \(= 0\).
(c) The kite is stationary, so the string tension, the weight and the force of the wind add to zero. Net force \(= 0\).
(d) The car moves with constant velocity, so the driving force is exactly balanced by friction and air resistance. Net force \(= 0\).
(e) The electron is far from all material objects and free of electric and magnetic fields, so no force acts on it at all. Net force \(= 0\).
Net force is zero in all five cases; note that in (a) to (d) the individual forces are non-zero but cancel, whereas in (e) there is genuinely no force acting.

Air resistance is ignored, so once the pebble leaves the hand the only force on it is its weight.
\(F = mg = 0.05 \times 10 = 0.5\,\text{N}\), directed vertically downwards.
(a) During upward motion: \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards.
(b) During downward motion: \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards.
(c) At the highest point: \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards. The velocity is momentarily zero there, but the force and hence the acceleration are not.
If the pebble is thrown at \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal the answers do not change, because gravity is still the only force acting. The one difference is that at the highest point the pebble is no longer at rest: it keeps a constant horizontal component of velocity throughout the flight.
(a) \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards; (b) \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards; (c) \(0.5\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards. Unchanged for a \(45^\circ\) throw, except that the pebble is then not momentarily at rest at the top.

The weight of the stone is \(mg = 0.1 \times 10 = 1\,\text{N}\).
(a) Once dropped, the stone is acted on only by gravity. Net force \(= 1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards.
(b) The train moves with constant velocity, so it is an inertial frame and nothing extra acts on the stone. Net force \(= 1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards, the same as in (a).
(c) The moment the stone is released it loses contact with the train, so the train's acceleration can no longer be communicated to it. The force at an instant depends on the situation at that instant, not on the history of the motion. Net force \(= 1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards, again the same as in (a).
(d) The stone rests on the floor and moves with the train, so it shares the train's horizontal acceleration of \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Its weight and the normal force cancel vertically, so the net force is horizontal and is supplied by friction from the floor: \(F = ma = 0.1 \times 1 = 0.1\,\text{N}\).
(a) \(1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards; (b) \(1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards; (c) \(1\,\text{N}\) vertically downwards; (d) \(0.1\,\text{N}\) horizontal, in the direction of the train's acceleration.

By the second law, the retarding force gives the body a constant acceleration opposite to its motion.
\(a = \dfrac{-F}{m} = \dfrac{-50}{20} = -2.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
Using \(v = u + at\) with \(v = 0\) and \(u = 15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\),
\(0 = 15 - 2.5\,t\)
\(t = \dfrac{15}{2.5} = 6.0\,\text{s}\)
The body takes \(6.0\,\text{s}\) to stop.

The direction of motion is unchanged, so the motion is one-dimensional and the acceleration is uniform.
\(a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{3.5 - 2.0}{25} = \dfrac{1.5}{25} = 0.06\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
By the second law,
\(F = ma = 3.0 \times 0.06 = 0.18\,\text{N}\)
The speed increases, so the force acts along the direction of motion.
\(F = 0.18\,\text{N}\), directed along the direction of motion.

The two forces are perpendicular, so their resultant follows from Pythagoras' theorem.
\(F = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100} = 10\,\text{N}\)
By the second law,
\(a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
The acceleration is parallel to the resultant force, which makes an angle
\(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{6}{8}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.75) = 37^\circ\)
with the direction of the \(8\,\text{N}\) force.
\(a = 2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), directed along the resultant, i.e. at \(37^\circ\) to the \(8\,\text{N}\) force.

The retarding force acts on the vehicle together with its driver, so the mass to use is
\(m = 400 + 65 = 465\,\text{kg}\)
Convert the initial speed: \(36\,\text{km/h} = \dfrac{36 \times 1000}{3600} = 10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\(a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{0 - 10}{4.0} = -2.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
By the second law the magnitude of the average retarding force is
\(F = ma = 465 \times 2.5 = 1162.5\,\text{N} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}\)
The average retarding force is \(1.2 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}\), opposite to the direction of motion.

Two vertical forces act on the rocket at lift-off: the upward thrust \(F\) and the downward weight \(mg\). By the second law,
\(F - mg = ma\)
\(F = m(g + a) = 20000 \times (10 + 5.0)\)
\(F = 20000 \times 15 = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N}\)
The initial thrust of the blast is \(3.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N}\), directed vertically upwards.

Take north as the positive direction. The force is directed south, so
\(a = \dfrac{-F}{m} = \dfrac{-8.0}{0.40} = -20\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), acting only for \(0 \le t \le 30\,\text{s}\).
At \(t = -5\,\text{s}\) the force has not yet been applied, so the body moves with uniform velocity:
\(x = ut = 10 \times (-5) = -50\,\text{m}\)
At \(t = 25\,\text{s}\) the force is still acting, so
\(x = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 10 \times 25 - 10 \times 625 = 250 - 6250 = -6000\,\text{m} = -6\,\text{km}\)
At \(t = 100\,\text{s}\) the force stops at \(t = 30\,\text{s}\), so treat the motion in two stages. For \(0\) to \(30\,\text{s}\),
\(x_1 = 10 \times 30 - 10 \times 900 = 300 - 9000 = -8700\,\text{m}\)
\(v = u + at = 10 - 20 \times 30 = -590\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
From \(30\,\text{s}\) to \(100\,\text{s}\) no force acts, so the velocity stays constant for \(70\,\text{s}\):
\(x_2 = -590 \times 70 = -41300\,\text{m}\)
\(x = x_1 + x_2 = -8700 - 41300 = -50000\,\text{m} = -50\,\text{km}\)
Positions (negative means south of the origin): at \(t = -5\,\text{s}\), \(x = -50\,\text{m}\); at \(t = 25\,\text{s}\), \(x = -6\,\text{km}\); at \(t = 100\,\text{s}\), \(x = -50\,\text{km}\).

The stone is released with whatever velocity the truck has at that moment. At \(t = 10\,\text{s}\),
\(v_x = 0 + 2.0 \times 10 = 20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), horizontal.
After release the only force on the stone is gravity, so by the first law its horizontal velocity stays \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), while gravity builds up a vertical component. One second later, at \(t = 11\,\text{s}\),
\(v_y = 0 + 10 \times 1 = 10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), vertically downwards.
(The stone is still in flight: falling \(6\,\text{m}\) needs \(t = \sqrt{2 \times 6/10} = 1.1\,\text{s}\).)
\(v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{20^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{500} = 22.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
at an angle \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{10}{20}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \approx 27^\circ\) below the horizontal.
(a) Velocity \(= 22.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), at \(\tan^{-1}(1/2)\) with the horizontal.
(b) Acceleration \(= 10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), vertically downwards, since gravity is the only force acting.

Once the string is cut the only force on the bob is its weight, so it becomes a freely falling body launched with whatever velocity it had at that instant.
(a) At an extreme position the bob is momentarily at rest, so its initial velocity is zero. With only a vertical force acting on a body starting from rest, it falls straight down: the trajectory is a vertical straight line.
(b) At the mean position the bob has its maximum speed, \(1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), directed horizontally. It then has a constant horizontal velocity and a constant downward acceleration \(g\), which is projectile motion: the trajectory is a parabola.
(a) The bob falls vertically downwards. (b) The bob follows a parabolic path.

The scale reads the force the man exerts on it, which by Newton's third law is equal and opposite to the normal force \(N\) exerted on the man by the scale. The reading in kilograms is \(N/g\).
(a) Uniform speed means zero acceleration, so \(N = mg = 70 \times 10 = 700\,\text{N}\); reading \(= 700/10 = 70\,\text{kg}\).
(b) Accelerating downwards at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\): \(mg - N = ma\), so \(N = m(g - a) = 70 \times (10 - 5) = 350\,\text{N}\); reading \(= 35\,\text{kg}\).
(c) Accelerating upwards at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\): \(N - mg = ma\), so \(N = m(g + a) = 70 \times (10 + 5) = 1050\,\text{N}\); reading \(= 105\,\text{kg}\).
(d) In free fall the lift and the man both accelerate downwards at \(g\), so \(N = m(g - g) = 0\); the scale reads zero. This is the state of weightlessness.
(a) \(70\,\text{kg}\); (b) \(35\,\text{kg}\); (c) \(105\,\text{kg}\); (d) zero.

Read the velocity off the graph as the slope of the position-time line in each interval.
For \(t < 0\): the graph is horizontal at \(x = 0\), so \(v = 0\).
For \(0 < t < 4\,\text{s}\): the line rises uniformly from \(0\) to \(3\,\text{m}\), so \(v = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
For \(t > 4\,\text{s}\): the graph is horizontal at \(x = 3\,\text{m}\), so \(v = 0\).
(a) In each of the three intervals the graph is a straight line, so the velocity is constant, the acceleration is zero and therefore the force on the particle is zero in all three intervals.
(b) Impulse equals the change in momentum, and the velocity changes abruptly only at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\,\text{s}\).
At \(t = 0\): \(J = m(v_{\text{after}} - v_{\text{before}}) = 4 \times (0.75 - 0) = 3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
At \(t = 4\,\text{s}\): \(J = 4 \times (0 - 0.75) = -3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
(a) Zero in all three intervals. (b) \(3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) at \(t = 0\) and \(3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) in the opposite direction at \(t = 4\,\text{s}\).

[Textbook ambiguity: the question refers to bodies A and B but never states which of them is the \(10\,\text{kg}\) mass and which the \(20\,\text{kg}\), and no figure accompanies it. The printed answer key sidesteps this the same way the answer below does — by naming the masses rather than the letters — so no reading is lost, but a student looking for an A/B assignment in the stem will not find one.] The surface is smooth, so the only horizontal forces are the applied force and the string tension. Both bodies move together with the same acceleration.
\(a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{600}{10 + 20} = \dfrac{600}{30} = 20\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) in both cases.
The tension is whatever force is needed to give the body that is NOT being pulled this acceleration, so it depends on which body the force is applied to.
If the \(20\,\text{kg}\) body is pulled, the string has to accelerate the \(10\,\text{kg}\) body:
\(T = 10 \times 20 = 200\,\text{N}\)
(Check on the pulled body: \(600 - T = 20 \times 20 = 400\), giving \(T = 200\,\text{N}\).)
If the \(10\,\text{kg}\) body is pulled, the string has to accelerate the \(20\,\text{kg}\) body:
\(T = 20 \times 20 = 400\,\text{N}\)
Acceleration is \(20\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) in each case. Tension \(= 200\,\text{N}\) when the \(20\,\text{kg}\) body is pulled, and \(400\,\text{N}\) when the \(10\,\text{kg}\) body is pulled. (The question does not state which of A and B is the heavier body, so the two cases are given by mass.)

The string is inextensible and the pulley frictionless, so both masses have the same magnitude of acceleration \(a\) and the tension \(T\) is the same throughout the string. The \(12\,\text{kg}\) mass descends and the \(8\,\text{kg}\) mass rises.
For the \(8\,\text{kg}\) mass (moving up): \(T - 8 \times 10 = 8a\)
For the \(12\,\text{kg}\) mass (moving down): \(12 \times 10 - T = 12a\)
Adding the two equations eliminates \(T\):
\(120 - 80 = 20a\), so \(a = \dfrac{40}{20} = 2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
Substituting back,
\(T = 8 \times 10 + 8 \times 2 = 80 + 16 = 96\,\text{N}\)
Acceleration \(= 2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) (the \(12\,\text{kg}\) mass downwards, the \(8\,\text{kg}\) mass upwards), and the tension in the string is \(96\,\text{N}\).

The nucleus is at rest, so its initial momentum is zero. Disintegration is caused by forces internal to the nucleus, and no external force acts on it in the laboratory frame, so the total momentum of the system is conserved.
Let the two product nuclei have momenta \(\mathbf{p}_1\) and \(\mathbf{p}_2\). Then
\(\mathbf{p}_1 + \mathbf{p}_2 = 0\), so \(\mathbf{p}_2 = -\mathbf{p}_1\)
The two momentum vectors are therefore equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Since each product has non-zero mass, its velocity is parallel to its momentum, so the two products must move along the same line in opposite directions.

Take the direction of motion of one ball as positive and consider that ball. Its speed is unchanged in magnitude but reversed in direction.
Initial momentum \(= mu = 0.05 \times 6 = 0.3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
Final momentum \(= -mu = -0.05 \times 6 = -0.3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
Impulse equals the change in momentum:
\(J = -0.3 - 0.3 = -0.6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
so its magnitude is \(2mu = 0.05 \times 12 = 0.6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) (i.e. \(0.6\,\text{N s}\)) in magnitude, and by Newton's third law the two impulses are equal and opposite in direction.

The gun and shell are initially at rest, and the forces between them are internal, so the total momentum of the system is conserved.
\(0 = m_{\text{shell}} v_{\text{shell}} + m_{\text{gun}} v_{\text{gun}}\)
\(0 = 0.020 \times 80 + 100 \times v_{\text{gun}}\)
\(v_{\text{gun}} = -\dfrac{1.6}{100} = -0.016\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
The recoil speed of the gun is \(0.016\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), i.e. \(1.6\,\text{cm s}^{-1}\), directed opposite to the motion of the shell.

Convert the speed: \(54\,\text{km/h} = \dfrac{54 \times 1000}{3600} = 15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The ball arrives at the batsman and is turned back, its outgoing path making \(45^\circ\) with the incoming path, and the speed is unchanged. Resolve along the bisector of the initial and final directions: each velocity makes an angle of \(45^\circ/2 = 22.5^\circ\) with that bisector. The components perpendicular to the bisector are equal and opposite and cancel, while the components along it both reverse, so
\(|\Delta p| = 2mv\cos 22.5^\circ\)
\(= 2 \times 0.15 \times 15 \times \cos 22.5^\circ\)
\(= 4.5 \times 0.9239 = 4.16\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\)
The impulse imparted to the ball is \(4.2\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) (i.e. \(4.2\,\text{N s}\)), directed along the bisector of the initial and final directions of the ball.
_note: The stem is ambiguous. Solved on the reading that the ball is turned back through the batsman, so the angle between the initial and final velocity VECTORS is \(135^\circ\) while the two paths are \(45^\circ\) apart as lines. If instead the velocity vector were taken to rotate by only \(45^\circ\), the impulse would be \(2mv\sin 22.5^\circ = 1.7\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

solution:
Convert the rate of revolution to a speed. In one minute the stone makes \(40\) revolutions, so
\(v = 2\pi R \times \dfrac{40}{60} = 2\pi \times 1.5 \times \dfrac{40}{60} = 2\pi\,\text{m s}^{-1} \approx 6.28\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
The tension supplies the centripetal force:
\(T = \dfrac{mv^2}{R} = \dfrac{0.25 \times 4\pi^2}{1.5} = \dfrac{9.87}{1.5} = 6.6\,\text{N}\)
For the maximum speed, set the tension to the breaking value \(200\,\text{N}\):
\(200 = \dfrac{mv_{max}^2}{R} = \dfrac{0.25\,v_{max}^2}{1.5}\)
\(v_{max}^2 = \dfrac{200 \times 1.5}{0.25} = 1200\,\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}\)
\(v_{max} = 34.6\,\text{m s}^{-1} \approx 35\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
The tension in the string is \(6.6\,\text{N}\) and the maximum speed is \(35\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
_note: Solved on the standard idealisation that the string lies in the horizontal plane so the whole tension is centripetal. A real stone whirled in a horizontal circle needs a vertical component of tension to balance its weight, which would make the string a conical pendulum and the tension slightly larger.

solution:
[Textbook defect: this question prints only THREE alternatives, not four. It ships here as a free-response question with the printed choices carried in the stem rather than as a multiple-choice question — inventing a fourth option would fabricate content the book does not contain.] While the stone moves in the circle its velocity is directed along the tangent at every instant; the tension merely supplies the centripetal force that continuously changes the direction of that velocity. When the string breaks the centripetal force disappears and no horizontal force acts on the stone any longer, so by Newton's first law it continues to move with the velocity it possessed at that instant, both in magnitude and in direction. That velocity is tangential.
The correct description is (b): the stone flies off tangentially from the instant the string breaks.
Alternative (a) is wrong because the stone never had a radially outward velocity, and (c) is wrong because the direction of the velocity at the moment of release is tangential whatever the speed.

(a) The horse pushes backwards on the ground and, by Newton's third law, the ground pushes forwards on the horse. It is this external forward force (friction from the ground) that accelerates the horse-and-cart system. The forces between the horse and the cart are internal to that system and cancel in pairs, so they cannot change its total momentum. In empty space there is no ground to push against, so no external force is available and the system cannot start moving.
(b) When the brakes are applied, the bus is retarded. The lower part of a passenger's body, in contact with the seat, is retarded along with the bus, but the upper part continues to move forwards with its original velocity because of inertia, no force having acted on it to stop it as quickly. Relative to the bus the passenger is therefore thrown forwards.
(c) The applied force is inclined to the horizontal. When the mower is pushed, the force has a downward component, which increases the normal reaction \(N\) beyond the weight; since friction \(f = \mu N\) grows with \(N\), a larger force is needed to move it. When it is pulled, the vertical component is upward, so \(N\) is less than the weight, the friction is smaller and a smaller force suffices. Hence pulling is easier.
(d) The ball's momentum has to be reduced to zero whichever way it is caught, so the change in momentum is fixed. By the second law the average force is \(F = \Delta p/\Delta t\). By drawing his hands back the cricketer increases the time \(\Delta t\) over which the momentum is destroyed, which reduces the force on his hands and prevents injury.
